messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amara is a 25-year-old Ethiopian-American surgical resident who presented for psychological assessment following a deployment-related trauma sustained during a medical humanitarian mission in a conflict zone approximately fourteen months ago. She had volunteered as part of a forward surgical team, and on a morning that began like any other — the smell of antiseptic, the weight of gloves being pulled over her hands — a series of coordinated explosions struck the perimeter of the field hospital. In the chaos that followed, she found herself working on casualties while aircraft circled overhead and secondary blasts continued to detonate nearby. What she cannot speak about in any coherent sequence — and what she has never been able to fully articulate to anyone, even in this intake — is what she saw and touched in those hours. The memory does not come to her in words. It comes in sensation: the particular give of damaged tissue beneath her gloved fingers, the vibration in her sternum from the concussive blasts, the sound of rotors cutting the air above a structure that no longer felt safe. She has told her supervising attending only that she "went through something overseas." She has told no one more than that.

Since returning to her residency program at a large urban hospital, Amara has found that the memory does not wait for her to summon it. It arrives unbidden, pulled forward by the world around her. The sound of a helicopter — and in a trauma centre, helicopters are not rare — can collapse the distance between then and now in an instant, flooding her with the same terror she felt pressed against that operating table fourteen months ago. A construction crew detonating something nearby last autumn sent her to the floor of a supply corridor before she had consciously registered what she was doing. Most insidiously, the texture of certain surgical materials — a particular grade of packing gauze, the specific resistance of a wound cavity — can return her without warning to a moment she cannot narrate but cannot escape. The memory, fragmented and nonverbal as it is, remains exquisitely sensitive to these sensory doorways, and the triggers it activates have begun to reshape her daily life in ways that are becoming impossible to conceal.

What has developed in response to these intrusions is a set of habits Amara thinks of, privately, as simply being careful. Before entering any room — a conference room, the hospital cafeteria, the OR anteroom — she identifies where the exits are. She does not sit with her back to a doorway under any circumstances; in the residents' lounge, she has quietly rearranged her routine so that she always occupies the corner seat facing the entrance, and colleagues have begun to notice and comment. She scans every environment she enters, reading faces, tracking movement, listening for anything that does not belong. She understands, on some level, that a hospital cafeteria is not a forward operating base. But the part of her that understands this is not the part that is in charge. What she has not yet recognised — and what is clinically significant — is that this constant vigilance keeps her perceptual system primed and sensitised, so that the very scanning she uses to feel safer makes her more likely to detect the sounds and sensations that send her back. The helicopters she listens for, she also hears first. The textures she braces against, she encounters with a nervous system already at threshold. The strategies that were meant to contain the triggers have become, over months, one of the mechanisms by which those triggers find her.

The consequence that finally brought her to seek help was not a flashback in the OR — though she fears that above almost everything else — but a formal notation in her performance review citing "difficulty with team communication and situational awareness during high-acuity cases." Amara, who had imagined herself defined by precision and composure, read those words and understood that what she was carrying had begun to cost her the thing she had built her life around. She came to this intake hoping to be told there is something specific that can be done, and terrified that what will be asked of her is to find words for something that, in her experience, has none.
